brief.idea: An unbundled peer-risk parametric rain micro-insurance platform that pays gig delivery couriers instantly via mobile money the second precipitation exceeds 3mm/hr in their geofenced sector.

audience.primary: Urban motorcycle, moped, and e-bike delivery couriers
audience.secondary: Independent fleet operators and delivery cooperatives
audience.context: Work in torrential monsoon/rain seasons where road danger surges and order demand drops or becomes hazardous, risking daily livelihood.

brief.problem: Traditional insurance requires days of paperwork, police reports, and claims adjusters, offering zero protection for immediate wage loss during flash storms.
brief.value: Automated hyper-local radar telemetry triggers instant payouts straight to mobile wallets within 90 seconds of a storm threshold breach, no claims needed.
constraints: No claim forms or human adjusters ever
Must not look like a sterile corporate insurance conglomerate or predatory payday loan
Zero financial jargon or confusing exclusions
open_questions: How to present rainfall threshold radar telemetry transparently on low-end smartphones?

qa.q: What is the core user experience when it starts pouring rain?
qa.a: The courier's phone buzzes with an instant mobile money transfer notification before their jacket is even wet.

qa.q: Why do couriers distrust existing insurance companies?
qa.a: Because insurers are designed to deny claims, demand receipts, and drag cases out for weeks.
Pay 50 cents per shift when storm probability is elevated; receive $25 instant wage stabilization payout if downpour occurs.

directions.positioning: Unapologetic algorithmic wage hedge for bad weather.

directions.name: RADARPAY
directions.name_rationale: Direct synthesis of Doppler radar trigger with immediate financial settlement.
directions.tagline: When it pours, your account fills.
directions.one_line_pitch: Automated rainfall wage defense that transfers cash to your phone the second downpours hit your delivery grid.

rules: Never refer to workers as 'heroes' or 'families'; treat them as independent commercial operators.
Talk about rain in millimeters per hour (mm/hr) and Doppler radar readings, never fuzzy weather forecasts.
Highlight speed of cash payout in exact seconds.
sample_messages: Precipitation at Sector 4 reached 3.4mm/hr. $22.50 credited to your wallet at 14:02:18.
Zero claims filed. Zero adjusters consulted. Telemetry confirmed.

typography.rationale: High-impact industrial headline paired with clean monospaced telemetry figures.

directions.label: Parametric Threshold Minimalist
directions.positioning: A binary contract with the sky.
directions.value_proposition: Precision rain trigger: 3mm of rain = $25 cash. Nothing else to understand.

traits.why: Either it rained 3mm or it did not. No nuance, no negotiations.
Functions like a circuit breaker for personal income.
Puts couriers in direct control of their shift risk.

directions.name: 3MM
directions.name_rationale: The exact physical rainfall threshold that triggers immediate cash payout.
directions.tagline: Three millimeters between storm and payout.
directions.one_line_pitch: Binary parametric rain protection paying out at exactly 3mm/hr rainfall threshold.

rules: Strip all clauses down to single-clause statements.
Treat insurance like physics rather than finance.
sample_messages: Threshold: 3.0mm/hr. Current reading: 3.2mm/hr. Trigger fired. Funds dispersed.

typography.heading: Space Grotesk
typography.rationale: Clean mathematical geometry with flawless mobile screen legibility.

visual.shape_language: Digital dials, liquid level gauges, precise millimeter crosshairs.
visual.image_style: Monochrome macro water droplet impacts on road surfaces.

revisions.reason: Replaced overused 'Shield' stem with physical metric definition.

directions.label: Courier Guild Protocol
directions.positioning: Mutual risk defense collective built by and for urban riders.

traits.why: Built on peer-to-peer solidarity rather than extractive insurance margins.
Forged in the reality of urban asphalt and winter squalls.
